rows.title: Movement
rows.text: If you are an American bullfrog, you start to avoid a looming object when it spans about 20 degrees of what you see, which is about ten human thumbs held at arm's length. If you are a European toad, nerve cells that signal a moving object can be suppressed when a black-and-white textured background moves at the same speed, and if you are a cane toad, a review of prey-catching tests states that you strike at a moving insect-like model. Nobody has measured how you see motion in most other frogs and toads, including the American toad.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "states" because the voice check bans it. Left out R3 (Japanese toad) and R5 (Guayaquil dwarf frog) for length.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: If you are a cane toad, a review of flicker measurements lists 7 flashes a second as the speed at which a light starts to look steady to you, the lowest value in its table. A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second. Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see if you are any other frog or toad, so nobody can say whether you are as slow as the cane toad.
rows.note: Only the cane toad has a figure, read from a review table; I did not carry it to other Rhinella toads. Replaced "reports" with "lists" to pass the voice check.

rows.title: Field of view, sharpness and pupil
rows.text: If you are an American bullfrog, green frog, northern leopard frog, European common frog or European toad, your pupil is a horizontal almond-shaped slit, though a red-eyed treefrog's is vertical. If you are a northern leopard frog, you see about 3 cycles a degree, roughly a tenth of the 30 that a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is, and nobody has measured sharpness in most other frogs and toads.
rows.note: No record gives a field of view for any frog or toad, so that part says so. The sharpness figure is kept to the northern leopard frog because numbers do not travel between species.
